title: Laurence Tratt: Another Non-Argument in Type Systems
summary: Tratt rebuts Harper's claim that dynamic typing is a straitjacketed special case of static typing: the encodings go both ways, sound static systems reject some correct programs, and expressiveness depends on which prism you use.

assertions.quote: The fundamental difference between statically and dynamically typed languages isn’t over how many types they have: it’s about when those types are utilised.

verdicts.note: Standard type-theory framing; the 'unityped' view is a legitimate static lens but says nothing about dynamic type counts.

Background definition only: static type systems check types at compile time while dynamic ones distinguish types at run time; the paper's gradual-typing method relies on JavaScript values having the same types either way.

assertions.quote: if the type system is sound then (because of the expressivity of programming languages) it will be incomplete, rejecting some programs

verdicts.note: Follows from undecidability; every practical sound type system is incomplete.

assertions.quote: a static type system forces us to explicitly express all the checks that a dynamically typed run-time implicitly performs for us

verdicts.note: True for naive sum-type encodings; gradual and inferred systems reduce but do not eliminate the annotation burden.

assertions.quote: Arguing whether static or dynamic typing is universally better or more expressive is therefore pointless.
They therefore can not replace static type systems, but can augment them.

verdicts.note: Industrial static analyzers deliberately trade soundness for coverage; this is their documented design position.

assertions.quote: ability to execute and run programs which are deliberately not statically type safe (a useful property when comprehending and modifying large systems)

verdicts.note: Running partially broken code aids exploration, but gradual typing and IDE tooling narrow the gap.
